column3: Conscious participation in harmful deeds makes conduct, not speech alone, morally visible.
Full repayment for what each soul did supplies an accountability horizon for the speech-deed gap.
Straight speech is urged as protective conduct, but the link is indirect after closer parallels.
The accusation that the message was invented foregrounds a false spoken claim.
The preceding identification of poets and their followers establishes the immediate setting for the critique.
A prophetic declaration of mission does not add to the mismatch between saying and doing.
Return for what disbelievers used to do makes deeds, rather than assertions, the measure.
The immediate exception defines believing poets through righteous action, sharply answering 26:226.
It directly repeats the question of why people say what they do not do.
Failure to restrain a wrong they committed joins corrupt action with neglected corrective speech.
Each side is separated by its own deeds, assigning responsibility beyond verbal dispute.
The question of who performed an act concerns agency, not whether speech matches conduct.
Patient withdrawal from hostile speech offers a response to words without addressing enacted inconsistency.
The immediate portrayal of poets wandering every valley gives the first half of their instability.
Remembrance must govern conduct; distraction that produces loss shows action can belie stated commitment.
Their tongues describe a false claim, furnishing a related case of speech detached from truth.
Seeking praise for what one did not do directly exposes claimed merit without matching action.
Divine action upon the elephant force does not clarify human speech without conduct.
The people's delayed compliance weakly illustrates words and action under command, but is less direct.
The command for straight speech presents the positive corrective to empty or errant speech.
Active concern with zakah is righteous conduct but adds no speech-action relation.
Appeal to inherited practice replaces a reasoned claim with repetition of what ancestors did.
Straight speech is explicitly connected to the repair of deeds, giving the constructive counterpart.
Moses acknowledges a past act, but this is accountability rather than a speech-deed discrepancy.
Pharaoh's complaint about the Israelites does not develop the focus theme.
A fulfilled divine matter and altered perception are not about speakers failing to act.
Knowledge of what people do makes actual deeds independently observable and accountable.
Patience before opponents' speech offers only a broad response to hostile words.
The conditional invitation to act has no meaningful connection to the focus.
Kind speech accompanies material care, but it does not illuminate inconsistency between claim and deed.
A mistaken expectation about resurrection is not developed as a speech-action problem.
Curse follows disobedience and transgression, providing the lead-in to their failure to forbid wrong.
Boastful speech converts possessions into self-assertion, a related risk of words outrunning reality.
Patience and praise in response to opponents' speech add little after similar cards.
Divine enabling of praise does not bear on people saying what they do not do.
The warning targets people who have spoken a false claim about God.
Expectation of return to the Lord does not add to the focus's speech-deed contrast.
The communal obligation and resulting disorder are too remote from the focus theme.
A companion corrects disbelief through creation, but the issue is not unperformed speech.
Private concealment and public claims expose a divide between what is said and what is inwardly held.
Failure to perform a required act is followed by concrete obligations, making conduct decisive.
A traveler's request for food has no useful relation to speech and action.
The comparison of communities does not clarify the focus's critique.
Reward for prior deeds gives a generic accountability frame already supplied more directly.
Divine effective willing is not a useful parallel to human unfulfilled speech.
Their recurring claim becomes testable when the reminder arrives, exposing speech as a prior assertion.
Beneficial speech is tied to charitable and reconciling action, a constructive but indirect parallel.
A verbal profession of faith without the corresponding reality closely parallels empty assertion.
Their spoken falsehood displays how a claim can issue from a prior distortion of truth.
The declared promise is recognized as fulfilled, providing a positive word-to-realization counterpart.
Moses' objection to an act does not address the reliability of speakers' claims.
Divine and human accountability differ, but this does not add to the focus's specific contrast.
The cry for escape at judgment does not concern speech that lacks action.
An apology for forgetting is not a significant connection to the focus.
The question about unbelief is too general to add to speech-deed inconsistency.
Directionless intoxicated wandering is only a remote analogue of the local poets' wandering.
Divine action against Aad does not illuminate the focus.
The denial of demonic suitability and ability is nearby but does not add to the critique of poets.
They speak with their tongues what is absent from their hearts, closely exposing insincere verbal excuse.
Shuayb's call to reverence is a local prophetic address but does not advance the focus theme.
A declarative falsehood is explicitly named a lie, offering another case of untrue speech.
Following desire and beautified evil work contrasts genuine evidence with conduct shaped by impulse.
The record of everything they did makes actual conduct persist beyond any verbal self-presentation.
Opponents' hurtful words are distinguished from their denial in action, giving a related speech-conduct divide.
A good word is shown to require truthfulness to God when the matter demands action.
Lot's plea against corrupters has no specific speech-action connection.
The hypothetical fabrication of speech is met with decisive consequence, underscoring the gravity of false utterance.
Peaceful speech in the Garden does not clarify unperformed claims.
Pharaoh turns one deed into an accusation; it is not about saying without doing.
The challenge to mute idols is about their inability to speak, not human inconsistency.
Past divine action made visible through examples offers only a distant accountability parallel.
The Lord's word of peace is effective speech, but it adds little to the human critique.
God knows what people do despite their reliance on conjecture, contrasting assertion with accountable conduct.
A true divine promise and righteous deeds are a broad positive contrast, but not a close link.
The confession of Lordship and divine support concern persecution rather than failed enactment.
Their repeated saying introduces a settled communal assertion, a related speech pattern.
Improper speech can nullify deeds, but this differs from speech lacking corresponding deeds.
The call joins a spoken declaration of divine oneness to righteous action and undivided worship.
An objectionable and false utterance is named as such, directly treating harmful speech as a moral act.
Calling visitors unfamiliar does not inform the focus.
The elite reduce the messenger to false labels, illustrating hostile speech that refuses the message's reality.
Their large utterance is explicitly unsupported by knowledge and identified as false speech.
The absence of idle or sinful speech in the Garden adds no material connection.
Past wrongdoing is recalled for recognition, but it does not center on claimed yet unperformed action.
God witnesses what they do after return, making deeds the final evidence.
A promise becomes a fulfilled event, a positive counterpart to words that fail realization.
The commanded prayer is wholesome speech but has no close speech-deed contrast.
The brothers' assurance that they will act is a direct promise whose fulfillment becomes narratively testable.
Satan's promises are explicitly deception, a close example of speech that does not deliver what it claims.
Appropriate speech is prescribed, but its link to enacted conduct is less direct than 33:70-71.
The question about emitted seed concerns divine creative agency, not human claims and conduct.
An invitation to look does not bear on saying without doing.
Satan promises protection, then withdraws when action is required, vividly enacting a false assurance.
The repeated labels of messenger as sorcerer or madman show inherited hostile speech replacing engagement with truth.
God's knowledge of what they invoke is too general to add after closer false-speech cards.
Their deeds will be reported after factional claims are set aside, making conduct the basis of judgment.
Unseen nearness at death does not concern spoken claims.
Gentle speech during inability to give is ethical communication, not a speech-deed mismatch.
The ban on ridicule and insulting labels regulates speech but does not concern unperformed claims.
Coordinated construction through commands does not add to the focus theme.
The immediate continuation declares it gravely hateful to God that people say what they do not do.
It rebukes those who direct others to righteousness while neglecting themselves, a direct speech-action contradiction.
Their response, "we hear and disobey," openly juxtaposes verbal reception with contrary conduct.
They ask for the command to fight, then most turn away when it is issued, making request fail in enactment.
Those who claim they would fight decline the actual summons, exposing an evasive spoken position.
They say obedience in the prophet's presence but devise contrary plans after leaving him.
Some profess belief with their mouths while their hearts have not believed, a close parallel to empty assertion.
They promise charity and righteousness if granted bounty, then withhold and turn away.
Breaking their promise to God and lying produces enduring hypocrisy, showing the consequence of an unfulfilled pledge.
They swear they said nothing although they uttered disbelief, joining false denial to their actual speech.
Their excuses are set beside deeds that God and His messenger will see, making conduct answer verbal defense.
Those who build a harmful mosque swear they intended good, while God witnesses their lie.
The command to fulfill covenants forbids making sworn words that later lack enacted fidelity.
They declare belief and obedience, yet a party turns away immediately afterward.
A prior covenant not to retreat is recalled when the trial tests whether the spoken commitment will hold.
The faithful are distinguished as those who fulfilled what they pledged to God, the positive counterpart.
Those who say their Lord is God and then remain steadfast model a claim carried into conduct.
The Bedouins claim belief but are told faith has not entered their hearts, directly qualifying an asserted identity.
True faith is described through steadfast belief and striving, giving conduct to the profession of faith.
Hypocrites promise expelled allies that they will leave and fight with them, yet they do neither.
The hypocrites' testimony about the messenger is formally correct but identified as lying, exposing speech without truthful commitment.
They use their oaths as a shield, turning speech into cover for conduct that diverts from God's way.
